sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Pandōra** (*pandora*) — First Woman, Box of Evils · All-gifted — belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "First Woman, Box of Evils". The name means "All-gifted"[^1].

**Pandōra** belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is associated with first woman, box of evils.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Pandōra** and serves its temple at [pandora.com](https://punicodex.com/pandora/). The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *pandora* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Greek as **Πανδώρα**. Etymologically it means "All-gifted"[^1].

The reconstructed proto-form is *pan- + *dōr-* (proto-indo-european, "all-gifted"). Greek Πανδώρα 'all-gifted', from πᾶν 'all' and δῶρον 'gift'; the first woman in Hesiod's Theogony.

The ASCII form *pandora* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Pandōra** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **p** → **P** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **d** → **d** — Same
- **o** → **ō** — Macron: long omega
- **r** → **r** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same

The canonical temple for this name is served at **pandora.com**[^2].

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.
Wörterbuch der griechischen Eigennamen, 3rd ed., 1863.

sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/pandora/** — Greek Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **P** — Initial character of the restored form Pandōra.
- **andōra** — Remainder of the name, preserving the distinctive marks of the Greek tradition.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'PANDORA' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Greek** — Pandōra, the restored Unicode form of the name

Pandōra is Tier 1 because the Greek form preserves distinctive features that ASCII loses: stress, length, or special characters.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The stories of **Pandōra** circulate within the Greek corpus, where the figure embodies first woman, box of evils.[^1]

### Primary Attestation (Sources)

Pandōra is attested in the canonical Greek sources as a figure associated with first woman, box of evils.[^2]

### Name and Meaning (Etymology)

The name means "All-gifted" and reflects the figure's role in the tradition. **Pandṓra** is the first woman in Hesiodic cosmogony, fashioned by the gods as a punishment for Prometheus's theft of fire. She opens the jar (*pithos*) and releases evils into the world, retaining only Hope.[^1] The story explains the origin of human suffering while framing womanhood within a pessimistic theological economics. The jar—often mistranslated as a box in later European retellings—was a storage vessel, and Hope's retention inside it has been debated since antiquity.[^2]

sources.citation: Wörterbuch der griechischen Eigennamen, 3rd ed., 1863.
Etymological Dictionary of Greek, 2 vols., Brill, 2010.

sections.body:
Pandōra appears within the Greek tradition and has influenced later retellings, artistic depictions, and scholarly study. The Unicode restoration preserves the name's distinctive orthography for contemporary use.[^1]

Within the Greek tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[acheron|Achérōn]], [[achilleus|Achilleús]], [[adamas|Adámas]], [[aer|Aḗr]], [[aither|Aithḗr]], and [[ananke|Anánkē]].

sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: Pandōra continues to appear in scholarship, art, and popular reception as a significant figure of the Greek tradition. Restoring the name in Unicode returns the original marks that ASCII removes.[^1] "Pandora's box" has become a proverb for unintended consequences and a recurring motif in literature, art, and political commentary.[^1]

sections.label: Homeric Hymns
sections.body:
The myth of **Pandōra** is told not in the Homeric Hymns but in the proem of **Hesiod's Works and Days** and in the **Theogony**, both of which stand in the hymnic tradition.[^1] Zeus commands Hephaistos to mould the first woman as punishment for Prometheus's theft of fire, and the gods heap gifts upon her.[^2]

Hesiod's account is the foundational "hymn" of Pandora, explaining why toil and disease fill the human world.

sources.citation: Hesiod, Works and Days 42–105.
Hesiod, Theogony 570–612.

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Epithets & Epicleses
sections.body:
Pandōra's name is itself an epithet: **Πανδώρα** (*Pandōra*, "all-gifted"), because every Olympian gave her a gift.[^1] In some contexts she is called **Ἀνησιδώρα** (*Anēsidōra*, "sender-up of gifts"), a title that distinguishes her gifts from the evils released from her jar.[^2]

Both names express the ambiguity of the first woman: she is bane and blessing inseparably united.

sources.citation: Hesiod, Works and Days 80–82.
Hesiod, Theogony 592.

sections.label: Oracle & Cult Sites
sections.body:
Pandōra had no major oracular sanctuary, but her myth is tied to **Thessaly**, where Prometheus shaped mankind from clay, and to the **Acropolis of Athens**, where a cult of Pandora was associated with Athena.[^1] The jar itself became a ritual object symbolizing the containment of misfortune.[^2]

Her absence from oracular sites underscores that she is a cosmic figure rather than a local goddess.

sources.citation: Pausanias, Description of Greece 1.24.7 (Pandora on the base of Athena Parthenos).
Hesiod, Works and Days 90–105.

sections.label: Iconography
sections.body:
Pandōra is shown as a **beautiful woman** holding a **large jar or pithos**, often accompanied by Hephaistos, Athena, Hermes, and Eros.[^1] The lid of the jar is her defining attribute: lifted, it releases evils; replaced, it traps only **Elpis** (Hope).[^2]

The scene was popular on Attic vases and later became a moral allegory in Renaissance art.

sources.citation: Lexicon Iconographicum Mythologiae Classicae (LIMC), s.v. Pandora.
Hesiod, Works and Days 94–99.

sections.body: Pandōra embodies first woman, box of evils in the Greek imagination. The name's restoration is not merely cosmetic: it recovers the stress, length, and script that make the figure recognizable in the source tradition.[^1]
